tidbits.text: In the 1730s, Charles Townshend promoted turnips in crop rotation so hard that people nicknamed him “Turnip” Townshend.

tidbits.source_pointer: 10.3 Casefile A, Day 2 Outside Information box

tidbits.source_pointer: 10.3 Casefile A, Day 4 Outside Information box

exemplars.text: After Parliament passed the enclosure acts, poor families lost the common land. By 1801, Arthur Young wrote that the poor were injured by nineteen enclosure bills in twenty.

After Parliament passed thousands of enclosure acts, families who had grazed animals on common land lost it, and many moved to towns to look for work. By 1801, Arthur Young - a well-known writer on farming who had spent years arguing FOR enclosure - put the cost to the poor in print anyway.
exemplars.what_changed: The 4 sets the scene and stops. The 5 says why THIS writer saying THIS, in THIS year, is worth quoting. Historical context is not only what was happening - it is what made this person write this down, then.

techniques.name: Name the turn
techniques.explanation: When a writer argues against his own side, say so. A supporter of enclosure admitting it hurt the poor is stronger context than any date, because it tells the reader why the document exists.

techniques.name: Start one step further back
techniques.explanation: Most answers begin at the event itself. Ask what caused the event and begin there instead. The exam asks for the circumstances that LED TO it, which means the sentence before the one you wanted to write.

try_it.prompt: Document 10 is a railway that opened in 1830. Write the historical circumstances that led to it - and start before the canals, not with them.
